summary:
Kostroma Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full. The regional assessment identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately, so the oblast is assessed at the national score.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned outright since 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed. Gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year, and same-sex marriage is banned. Same-sex sexual activity as such is not criminalised.

The 2013 propaganda law is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. The expanded law criminalises any public expression that justifies gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and national government warnings expressly direct LGBT travellers to that risk.

Since the Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising six to ten. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, about 98 of them administrative and three criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. Cases under the propaganda laws have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the extremist designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 on a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Travel advisories reflect the same position. The US State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention risk, the war and arbitrary law enforcement, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch called on governments on 30 June 2025 to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia in the wake of the extremism designation, framing the risk as one that drives outward movement rather than only domestic exposure.

The UK Home Office note sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims and treats LGBT+ people in Russia as a particular social group, which matters for a visitor who decides not to return rather than for the visit itself.

The US Level 4 advisory applies to all travellers regardless of personal characteristic and cites wrongful detention, the war and arbitrary law enforcement, so trans-specific exposure sits inside a broader country-wide warning rather than beside it.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025 according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.
localsOnly:
The UK Home Office note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them.

Residents carry the heavier end of the criminal exposure: participation in the designated movement carries two to six years and organising six to ten, publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 face up to 12 years, and article 20.3 supplies an administrative route that produced 98 convictions in the period covered.

No domestic route exists for legal gender recognition or for gender-affirming care, and markers on official documents cannot be changed, so a resident's documents will continue to present the sex assigned at birth.

Fines under the propaganda statutes have functioned as a revenue line, bringing more than 60 million rubles into the state budget across two years, which indicates routine rather than exceptional enforcement.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kostroma Oblast-specific enforcement data, arrests, court decisions or police conduct is present in the source inventory; the regional assessment identified no deviation from the national position, and the national score is adopted on that basis rather than on local evidence of safety.

The conversion-therapy detention documented by BBC Russian took place near Novosibirsk, not in Kostroma Oblast, and evidences a national pattern of coercion rather than a local one.

Whether oblast-level police or courts in Kostroma have applied the extremist designation, the propaganda statutes or article 20.3 locally is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

Access to any LGBT-friendly venues, healthcare or support organisations within Kostroma Oblast is not covered by the inventory and is not asserted either way.
